extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of classical literature; writers and critics studying poetic theory and dramatic composition
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts evaluative principles for poetry, tragic drama, and style drawn from a historical/critical survey of Greek literature (discussion of poets, dramatists, and philosophical influence). Useful for guiding creative-writing decisions about invention, expression, unity, and rhetorical artifice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essence of poetry — Invention, Expression, Inspiration
rubrics_metrics.description: "The essence of all poetry may be said to consist in three things, INVENTION, EXPRESSION, INSPIRATION."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A great inventive genius will usually have the other two elements; but without creative invention a work may still be poetic by strong expression or by powerful inspiration. These three are presented as the constituent parts of poetry and a criterion for judging poetic merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary national function — preserve traditions and recollections
rubrics_metrics.description: "The first and original end of all poetry ... is, to preserve and embellish the peculiar traditions and recollections of the people; and to preserve alive, in the memories of men, the magnanimity and greatness of ages that are gone by."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epic narrative is identified as the most fitting mode for this function because it permits the marvellous and mythology required to sustain national tradition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary function — represent common life with higher meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry's second end is to "place before our eyes a clear and speaking picture of common life."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drama is especially powerful for this purpose, but such representations must be "intermingled with something of a higher nature" — intellect and feeling — so that the depiction of ordinary life attains poetic value and is not mere reportage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry must contain an element of the higher or inspired
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry "must always be intermingled with something of a higher nature, and have for its object the intellect and feeling of which that life is the symbol."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pure external representation without this higher element is judged insufficient; the presence of inspiration elevates representations of common life toward lyric or poetic status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invisible art — conceal the labour of composition
rubrics_metrics.description: "The art which is employed in writing should indeed be kept, as much as possible, out of view."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visible labour or excessive polish in writing is "instantly, and invariably, disagreeable." Works should feel free, lively, and influential on life rather than obviously 'hewn' by toil; visible artifice is an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy of expression without ostentation
rubrics_metrics.description: While extreme refinement of language can be useful, the writer must avoid making expression an end in itself; accuracy of expression is important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text contrasts useful attention to expression with sophistical artifice (e.g., Isocrates' affected rhetoric). Choose words carefully for clarity and force, but avoid conspicuous verbal ostentation that displaces substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity between choral and dramatic parts in tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: "Perfect harmony and agreement between the choral songs, and the dramatic part — strictly so called, forms, in tragedies composed after these models, a requisite altogether indispensable."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In ancient-style tragedy the chorus is integral (originating in festival song); choral odes must be in unison with the action. Sophocles exemplifies this harmony; Euripides is criticized when choruses become unrelated vehicles for private opinions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain unity and connection of parts; avoid loose structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy (and poetic composition generally) should have unity and connection between its parts; lack of unity is a principal defect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Euripides' principal defect is described as "a want of unity and connection between the different parts"; remedies like convoluted plots, perpetual surprises, recognitions, double catastrophes are criticized as incompatible with true tragic dignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of lyrical interludes
rubrics_metrics.description: Choral interludes should relate to the events of the drama rather than serving as ostentatious displays or unrelated dogmas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When lyrical passages become 'vehicles' for the poet's private opinions or pedantic disquisitions, they disturb the harmony of the piece and make the dialogue poor and unsatisfactory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match form to purpose — epic for the marvellous, drama for common life
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic narrative is best suited to the introduction of the marvellous and mythology; drama is most powerful for representing common life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose genre and form according to the poem's aim: national/mythic preservation leans epic; vivid depiction of everyday life suits drama. Misplacing material (e.g., overlearned myth-collection) produces artificiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid learned-obscurity and purely erudite poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Learned poets (e.g., Alexandrian court poets) often have modes of expression that are "rarely unaffected, and very often altogether obscure."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive erudition and formalism can make poetry obscure and lifeless; scholarship should serve clarity and poetic force rather than become the poem's substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style qualities: variety, purity, elegance, and dignity of reflection
rubrics_metrics.description: Good writers combine purity and elegance (Aristotle), unrivalled variety adapting to both abstract and poetical modes (Plato), and simplicity and natural feeling (Xenophon).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess style by its suitability to subject and effect: elegance and purity favor erudition and historical composition; variety and expressive power favor narrative and dialogue; simplicity can give clarity and beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetorical artifice as anti-pattern — sophistical manner
rubrics_metrics.description: Sophistical rhetoric selects and arranges words and periods with laborious care, making reason subservient to pleasure; sophists 'made the worse appear the better reason' and used rhetoric to deceive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid rhetoric that prizes clever turns and sound over substance; such artifice undermines moral and intellectual seriousness and corrupts the effect of writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coherent handling of mythological material
rubrics_metrics.description: Treating mythological events in a merely formal manner by collecting similar fictions into one work is vain when there is no real connection between them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizing myths into a consecutive order without natural links requires artificial omissions and interlacings (critical example: Ovid's Metamorphoses). Ensure mythic material has organic coherence.
